claim: Typical raised bogs are domed, ombrotrophic peat landforms confined to a climatic band: cool enough to limit decomposition, productive enough for Sphagnum peat to accumulate; colder/wetter they give way to fens, aapa mires and blanket bogs, warmer/drier to forest, heath and farmland
The typical raised bog region of Europe (mire region IV) and Norway as its north-western outpost: Norway's raised bogs sit at the cool end of the band
Earlier bioclimatic-envelope or distribution models for bogs and mires, what they projected, and their limits (binary response, coarse grain, extrapolation)
Observed and projected climate-change impacts on bog hydrology, Sphagnum growth and peat accumulation (drying, water-table drawdown, shrub encroachment, carbon loss)
Management context: restoration prioritisation in Norway, Natura 2000 habitats 7110/7120, and why climate-informed conservation needs to know which bogs keep their climate
Truncated niches: a model trained within one country cannot see the warm edge of the niche when the country does not contain it; pooling data across the range as the remedy
Multiclass (three-class) response in distribution modelling of habitats or ecosystems; a binary model lumps two opposite flanks into one negative class
Balanced random forest for imbalanced classes; default hyperparameters are adequate; a forest fitted under a rebalanced prior yields scores, not calibrated prevalence
Random cross-validation overstates skill under transfer; environmental / feature-space blocking along the axis the projection travels

Justification for using a single GCM (GFDL-ESM4) and the two scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0)

Uncertainty from one climate model; scenario versus GCM spread in ecological impact projections
